title: Normalize Messy Price Rows into Clean JSON
scenario: It is 6:20 AM. A price feed dropped overnight rows into the system, but the values are messy strings with currency symbols and units. Risk Evaluation cannot do math on "$187/MWh". Your job is to normalize the rows into a clean, numeric table the rest of the workflow can trust.
input:
hub, peak, settled
ercot, $187/MWh, $142/MWh
SPP, $96/MWh, $88/MWh
miso, $74 /MWh, $70/MWh
instructions: Read the raw price rows and note each hub and its prices.
Build a JSON array with one object per hub.
Give each row hub, peakPrice, and settledPrice.
Convert prices to plain numbers - strip the $ sign and the /MWh unit.
Keep all three hubs (ERCOT, SPP, MISO), then validate.
copilotPrompt: Normalize these raw price rows into a JSON array. Each object should have hub, peakPrice, and settledPrice. Convert the prices to plain numbers with no currency symbol or unit.
successMessage: Clean price table built. Risk Evaluation and the Morning Brief can now run math on trusted numeric values.

intro.heading: Before you build: normalization and data quality

sections.title: What normalization is
sections.body: Normalization means reshaping messy values into one consistent form. Here, every price becomes a plain number so any later step can compare or calculate without re-parsing text. (Domain note: a hub is a regional power-trading point; $/MWh is the price of one megawatt-hour of electricity; the settled price is the final cleared price for the day.)

sections.title: Type coercion
sections.body: "$187/MWh" is a string, not a number. Software cannot safely add or compare it. Coercion strips the formatting and stores the real numeric value: 187.

sections.title: Data quality is a trust boundary
sections.body: Everything downstream trusts this table. If a price is left as a string or a row is dropped, Risk Evaluation inherits the error. Cleaning the data once protects every later step.

sections.title: Where this fits
sections.body: Clean Price Data sits in Phase 2, the Data Structure Layer. Its clean-prices.json feeds Risk Evaluation and the Morning Brief.

realWorld.soloRebuildPath: By hand you'd find-and-replace the '$' and '/MWh' out in Excel, then set the column type to number so formulas work.

tools.powerAutomate: 'Apply to each' row with replace()/int() expressions to coerce values
tools.zapier: 'Formatter > Numbers' to strip symbols and convert text to a real number
tools.python: float(re.sub(r'[^0-9.]', '', value)) per cell, or pandas.to_numeric

takeaway.heading: Clean price table built
points: You normalized messy price strings into a numeric JSON table.
Type coercion turned values like "$187/MWh" into the number 187 that automation can compute on.
This artifact sits in Phase 2, the Data Structure Layer, of the Meridian workflow map.
Risk Evaluation and the Morning Brief reuse clean-prices.json downstream.
The workflow can now perform deterministic calculations on trusted numeric prices.
